variants.title: Run the measurement path
variants.context: A reasoning score is the output of a complete measurement path: define the construct, build independent items, freeze the protocol, then report a bounded result. Each stage narrows what the final number may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: A team wants to claim that a model handles multi-step arithmetic reliably under tool use. Put the stages of the measurement path in order.

items.text: Freeze the protocol by pinning the model, prompt, tools, sampling, reasoning budget, retries, parser, and scorer.
Define the construct by naming the observable tasks, difficulty range, constraints, and failure modes that count as multi-step arithmetic.
Build independent items with versioned examples, a protected split, named slices, and controlled variants that expose shortcuts.
Report a bounded result with item counts, slice uncertainty, cost, failures, and explicit limits on generalization.

variants.hint: The claim decides the questions, and the questions are written before anything is run.
variants.explanation: Each stage narrows what the score may claim, so items written after the protocol is pinned cannot repair a vague construct.

variants.title: Run the measurement path
variants.context: A reasoning score is the output of a complete measurement path: define the construct, build independent items, freeze the protocol, then report a bounded result. Each stage narrows what the final number may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: A safety-critical exception-handling slice must be added to a suite that already ships. Put the work in order.

items.text: Author protected items for the slice, including derivations and controlled variants, and keep them out of development data.
Publish the slice pass count, attempt count, and interval beside the aggregate instead of folding it into the mean.
State which exception-handling behaviors the new slice must observe and which failures are unacceptable.
Pin the run configuration for the slice, including its parser, scorer, and minimum item count, before the final execution.

variants.hint: A new slice repeats the whole path rather than borrowing the old protocol's authority.
variants.explanation: A slice added without its own construct, protected items, pinned protocol, and reported uncertainty cannot carry a safety claim.

variants.title: Run the measurement path
variants.context: A reasoning score is the output of a complete measurement path: define the construct, build independent items, freeze the protocol, then report a bounded result. Each stage narrows what the final number may honestly claim.
variants.prompt: A team inherits a vendor benchmark reporting 91 percent and wants to reuse it for a code-review assistant. Put the work they still owe in order.

items.text: Inspect the vendor items for coverage, ambiguity, and exposure, then build the missing protected items.
Write the code-review behaviors, users, and unacceptable failures the 91 percent number would have to represent.
Pin the assistant's own model, prompt, tool access, and scorer rather than reusing the vendor run configuration.
Publish a result that names the items, protocol version, costs, and the claims the evidence does not support.

variants.hint: An inherited number describes the vendor's measurement path, not this product's.
variants.explanation: A score transfers only when construct, items, protocol, and scoring rule all match the new claim.

variants.title: Run a controlled pair
variants.context: A controlled perturbation changes one defined property of an item while holding the rest constant. The expected relationship between the two reference answers is written before any model output is inspected, and pair identifiers stay linked so the comparison uses paired outcomes.
variants.prompt: An evaluator suspects the model keys on surface tokens rather than the stated rule. Put the steps of the paired test in order.

items.text: Compare the linked pair outcomes rather than two separate aggregate rates.
Run the original item and its variant under the same frozen protocol and keep the pair identifier attached to both.
Write the expected relationship, that the conclusion should be preserved, before any model output is read.
Record an unexpected flip as a pair failure and route the transcript to review.
Change one defined property, an arbitrary entity rename, and hold wording, format, and difficulty constant.

variants.hint: Which step must happen before anyone can see how the model answered?
variants.explanation: Writing the expected relation first, then comparing linked outcomes, is what turns two items into evidence about a shortcut.

variants.title: Run a controlled pair
variants.context: A controlled perturbation changes one defined property of an item while holding the rest constant. The expected relationship between the two reference answers is written before any model output is inspected, and pair identifiers stay linked so the comparison uses paired outcomes.
variants.prompt: A reviewer wants to know whether the model updates after a premise is reversed. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Count an unchanged answer as invalid invariance and keep the pair in the failure record.
Reverse the premise in one item while leaving the entities, numbers, and format untouched.
Declare that the reference conclusion must change in the specified direction, and record that before the run.
Check each linked pair for the required change rather than averaging the two items separately.
Execute both items with the same model version, prompt, tools, and sampling settings.

variants.hint: A meaning-changing intervention has an expected direction, not just an expected difference.
variants.explanation: Invalid invariance is only visible when the required change was declared in advance and outcomes stay paired.

variants.title: Run a controlled pair
variants.context: A controlled perturbation changes one defined property of an item while holding the rest constant. The expected relationship between the two reference answers is written before any model output is inspected, and pair identifiers stay linked so the comparison uses paired outcomes.
variants.prompt: An author proposes a transformation that two domain reviewers read differently. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Notice that reviewers disagree about which conclusion the variant requires.
Apply the proposed transformation to the original item and describe exactly what it changed.
Attempt to write one expected relationship between the two reference answers.
Send the pair back for review instead of scoring it, because an ambiguous transformation is not a robustness test.
Return the repaired pair to the suite only once a single expected relationship is agreed and recorded.

variants.hint: What should happen when the expected relationship cannot be written down?
variants.explanation: An ambiguous transformation produces reviewer disagreement, not model error, so it is repaired before it can score anything.

variants.title: Compute the aggregate the claim needs
variants.context: Benchmark composition is the mix of capabilities and difficulty in the test items. A naive aggregate divides total passing items by total attempted items, while a target-weighted aggregate multiplies each slice score by its declared deployment weight.
variants.prompt: A four-slice suite reports pass rates of 90, 70, 60, and 40 percent. The declared deployment weights are 40, 30, 20, and 10 percent in the same order. What is the target-weighted aggregate?
variants.hint: Each slice contributes its rate scaled by the population it represents.
variants.explanation: The target-weighted aggregate multiplies every slice score by its declared weight, so a heavy easy slice cannot silently set the headline.

mistakes.feedback: That is the unweighted mean of the four rates, which gives a 10 percent slice the same influence as a 40 percent slice.
You paired the weights with the slices in reverse order.

variants.title: Compute the aggregate the claim needs
variants.context: Benchmark composition is the mix of capabilities and difficulty in the test items. A naive aggregate divides total passing items by total attempted items, while a target-weighted aggregate multiplies each slice score by its declared deployment weight.
variants.prompt: The same suite reports 180 of 200 routine items passing, 70 of 100 multi-step items, 30 of 50 distractor items, and 20 of 50 counterfactual items. What is the naive aggregate?
variants.hint: The naive view counts items, not slices.
variants.explanation: The naive aggregate divides total passing items by total attempted items, so the slice with the most sampled items dominates it.

mistakes.feedback: That is the unweighted mean of the four slice rates, which ignores how many items each slice contributed.
That is the failure rate; the naive aggregate divides passing items by attempted items.

variants.title: Compute the aggregate the claim needs
variants.context: Benchmark composition is the mix of capabilities and difficulty in the test items. A naive aggregate divides total passing items by total attempted items, while a target-weighted aggregate multiplies each slice score by its declared deployment weight.
variants.prompt: A rebalanced suite reports slice rates of 84, 64, 50, and 40 percent with deployment weights of 50, 20, 20, and 10 percent in the same order. What is the target-weighted aggregate?
variants.hint: Multiply before you add, and check that the weights total 100.
variants.explanation: Reweighting changes the headline without changing any slice rate, which is why the weights belong in the report beside the number.

mistakes.feedback: That is the unweighted mean of the four rates, not the target-weighted aggregate.
You applied the weights in reverse order, giving the weakest slice the largest share.

variants.title: Pick the strongest practical checker
variants.context: A scorer converts one system output into a structured result. Choose the least subjective checker that fully represents the task: a deterministic check where correctness is mechanically decidable, an expert rubric for bounded judgment, and a validated model-assisted grader when volume demands automation.
variants.prompt: Items ask the system to write a Python function, and a hidden test suite already exists for every item. Which scorer should the protocol use?
options: Run the hidden tests in an isolated environment and score exit status and side effects.
Ask a model-assisted grader whether the submitted code looks correct.
Have two reviewers rate the code for readability on a five-point rubric.
optionFeedback: Correct: execution is mechanically decidable here, so the least subjective checker fully represents the task.
A grader adds judgment and cost when a deterministic executable check is already available.
Readability ratings measure a different construct than whether the function solves the task.
variants.hint: Which checker fully represents the task with the least judgment?
variants.explanation: Use the least subjective checker that still represents the task, and store the raw output, parse status, and scorer version separately.

variants.title: Pick the strongest practical checker
variants.context: A scorer converts one system output into a structured result. Choose the least subjective checker that fully represents the task: a deterministic check where correctness is mechanically decidable, an expert rubric for bounded judgment, and a validated model-assisted grader when volume demands automation.
variants.prompt: Items ask for a short numeric answer with units, and the model sometimes buries the value in a sentence. Which scorer should the protocol use?
options: An expert rubric that scores how clearly the answer explains its calculation.
A rule that marks the item correct whenever the response contains the target digits.
Normalized match with a numeric tolerance and units, recording the parse status per item.
optionFeedback: A rubric adds reviewer judgment to a task whose correctness is already decidable.
Substring matching passes answers that merely mention the number, so it grades the parser, not the model.
Correct: the answer is mechanically decidable, and a stored parse status keeps formatting failures visible.
variants.hint: Parsing belongs inside the measurement path, not outside it.
variants.explanation: Store raw response, parsed answer, parse status, score, and scorer version separately so a parser regression is not read as a model regression.

variants.title: Pick the strongest practical checker
variants.context: A scorer converts one system output into a structured result. Choose the least subjective checker that fully represents the task: a deterministic check where correctness is mechanically decidable, an expert rubric for bounded judgment, and a validated model-assisted grader when volume demands automation.
variants.prompt: Ten thousand open-ended design answers must be scored weekly, and reviewer capacity covers only a few hundred. What is the defensible design?
options: Let the grader choose its own prompt each week so it adapts to new answer styles.
Use a model-assisted grader validated against a blinded human sample, with its model and prompt pinned.
Switch to exact match against one reference answer so the whole run is cheap and deterministic.
optionFeedback: An unpinned grader prompt makes every run a different instrument, so results are no longer comparable.
Correct: automation is acceptable once it is calibrated against human review and its version is pinned.
Exact match against a single reference rejects valid alternative answers and changes the construct.
variants.hint: Automation is allowed once its agreement with human review is measured.
variants.explanation: Validate a model-assisted grader against a human-reviewed set, pin its model and prompt, and report disagreement by slice.

variants.title: Name the part and what it covers
variants.context: Reasoning evidence is reported as separate parts with distinct jobs. Keeping them separate is what lets a reader see whether a system was correct, checkable, stable, and affordable rather than only one of those.
variants.prompt: Match each measurement dimension to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Outcome
pairs.detail: Was the final answer correct against an exact target, executable check, verifier, or rubric?

pairs.label: Process evidence
pairs.detail: Were the intermediate steps externally checkable, such as equations, code runs, or cited evidence?

pairs.label: Robustness
pairs.detail: Did behavior survive meaning-preserving and meaning-changing controls?

pairs.label: System cost
pairs.detail: What did success require in attempts, tokens, latency, tool calls, and money?

variants.hint: Ask what each dimension would still hide if it were the only one reported.
variants.explanation: Keeping the four dimensions separate is what distinguishes a correct answer reached by an invalid path from one that is stable and affordable.

variants.title: Name the part and what it covers
variants.context: Reasoning evidence is reported as separate parts with distinct jobs. Keeping them separate is what lets a reader see whether a system was correct, checkable, stable, and affordable rather than only one of those.
variants.prompt: Match each external contract to the kind of work it can check.

pairs.label: Execute
pairs.detail: Run code in an isolated environment and score tests, side effects, limits, and exit status.

pairs.label: Verify
pairs.detail: Check units, equations, proofs, or symbolic state transitions with a trusted verifier.

pairs.label: Review
pairs.detail: Apply an explicit rubric with blinded reviewers, adjudication, and measured agreement.

pairs.label: Probe
pairs.detail: Intervene on hints, premises, and traces, then compare behavior instead of trusting the trace.

variants.hint: Each contract replaces trust in the visible text with something outside the model.
variants.explanation: A reasoning trace is a testable artifact, so prefer evidence with an external contract over a fluent explanation.

variants.title: Name the part and what it covers
variants.context: Reasoning evidence is reported as separate parts with distinct jobs. Keeping them separate is what lets a reader see whether a system was correct, checkable, stable, and affordable rather than only one of those.
variants.prompt: Match each paired outcome to the diagnosis it supports.

pairs.label: Flip after an entity rename
pairs.detail: Prompt sensitivity: the conclusion tracked surface tokens rather than the stated rule.

pairs.label: No change after a reversed premise
pairs.detail: Invalid invariance: the system did not update after the meaning changed.

pairs.label: Reviewer disagreement about the variant
pairs.detail: An ambiguous transformation that belongs back in review rather than in the score.

variants.hint: Two of these are model failures and one is an item defect.
variants.explanation: Paired analysis names which examples changed, which an unpaired accuracy difference can never show.
